top.answer: About 16 m, or 52 feet. That is the megalodon whose backbone lies in Brussels, the only long one ever found. Our 16 m is a little over nine people of 1.70 m laid head to foot. The largest of its kind were perhaps about 20 m (66 feet), by their teeth.
top.answer_more: Its weight is disputed: roughly 30 tonnes in the slim model of 2025, about twice that in the thicker model of 2022, because nobody knows the shape of its body.

guess.q: How long was a megalodon at birth?
guess.a: About 3.6 to 3.9 m (12 to 13 ft), by a growth model of 2025, more than twice the person of 1.70 m. That is a model, not a measured newborn, so take it as an estimate.

paras: Megalodon, Otodus megalodon, was a shark, and sharks have no bones. Their skeleton is cartilage, and cartilage almost always rots away in the ground. What survives are the teeth, and sometimes the backbone discs, which are harder than the rest. So megalodon is known from teeth, loose backbone discs, scraps of hardened cartilage and tiny skin scales. No body has ever been found, no head, no fin, no tail.

paras: The 16 m figure rests on the backbone in Brussels: 141 discs, about 11 m (36 ft) in a row, plus a head and a tail in the proportions of living mackerel sharks. Two research groups got 15.9 m and 16.4 m with different models, which is why we say about 16 m. The 20 m figure rests on a single tooth, scaled up through whole tooth sets. The weight rests on a body model, and that needs a body shape nobody knows: slim like the largest living sharks gives about 30 tonnes, stout like a great white about 61. That is why the length says “about” and the weight says “disputed”.

In Brussels, at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, lie 141 loose backbone discs of a single shark, IRSNB P 9893, found near Antwerp in the 1860s. The largest is 15.5 cm across, and in a row they run about 11 m. They give the trunk's length, not the head and not the body's girth. No teeth were found with them, so even the name megalodon for this animal is an inference.

In Denmark, remains of about 20 discs were dug up at Gram in 1978, then damaged in storage in 1989 and long thought lost. Two broken discs and many fragments survive. The larger disc is 23 cm (9 in) across, and the largest estimate in the list below rests on it.
Nobody has found a megalodon skeleton, and nobody has found a set of teeth still in place in the jaw. Every row of teeth you have ever seen is an arrangement, ours too.

blocks.intro: For each number: where it came from, and what the field makes of it now.

rows.text: The tooth method. A tooth's crown, scaled up to a body with the great white's proportions. Studies from 1996 to 2019 got 14 to 18 m that way, and the American Museum of Natural History still says roughly 15 m. By the study of 2025, such tooth rules give lengths that are too short or unreliable.

Perez, Leder and Badaut, 2021. The summed width of a tooth set's crowns, set against body length and applied to the widest tooth known: a mean of 20.0 m, a range of 17.4 to 23.5 m. The authors of the 2022 model accept 20 m as the maximum.

rows.term: 24 to 25 m (79 to 82 feet) and about 94 tonnes
rows.text: Shimada and others, 2025 and 2026. The Brussels model scaled up to a Danish disc of 23 cm: 24.3 m, and with the slim body about 94 tonnes. The authors call it hypothetical. It rests on the larger of two broken Danish discs and a single step of arithmetic.

Cooper and others, 2022. A 3D body of a great white, adjusted with five living mackerel sharks and stretched over the Belgian backbone, came to 61,560 kg. The heaviest published estimate of our animal. The slim model of 2025 gets about 30 tonnes for the same backbone, and the two count the body differently: a slimmer shape, the fins other than the tail left out, another density. The weight stays disputed.

At the American Museum of Natural History, fossil teeth were set in 1909 into a restored jaw scaled up from a great white. The museum itself says today that the restoration overestimated the size by far. As later experts found, teeth as large as the front ones ran all along the jaw, even where a real jaw holds small ones.

blocks.nav: Why our megalodon looks like this
blocks.h: Why our megalodon looks like this
paras: It is slim, after the model of 2025: a stout body like a great white's might have cost it too much effort to swim, its authors say, and the largest living sharks are slim. It is painted dark above and pale below, as living open-water sharks are, because the real colour is unknown. The teeth are built after another find, UF-VP-311000, a real set, at its own size. The head, the fins and the tail are borrowed from living mackerel sharks, because no megalodon head has ever been found. It is not a great white scaled up: it belonged to its own family, now extinct, and by the newest work it was slimmer and more drawn out than the monster in the film.

items.q: Megalodon vs great white: how much bigger was it?
items.a: The largest great whites reach about 6 m (20 ft), and a grown one is usually 4 to 5 m. So our megalodon of about 16 m was roughly two and a half to three times as long as the largest great white.

items.q: Megalodon vs blue whale: which was bigger?
items.a: The blue whale. Most grown blue whales are 23 to 27 m long, the largest about 30 m (98 ft), and NOAA, the US ocean agency, calls it the largest animal known to have lived. Our megalodon would come to a little over half of the largest. Even the largest whale shark ever measured, 18.8 m, was longer than our megalodon, and at about 34 tonnes about as heavy as the slim model of it.

The biggest found are at least 16 cm (6.3 in) tall, and museums give almost 18 cm (7 in), about three times a great white's tooth of about 5 cm. The teeth in our model are built after a real set from another find, UF-VP-311000, about 10 cm (4 in) tall in front and smaller toward the corners.

items.q: When and why did megalodon die out?
items.a: About 3.6 million years ago, by the youngest reliable fossils. Why is not settled. The proposals are cooling seas that broke up its range, the newly evolved great white as a rival, a fall in the small baleen whales it hunted, and the cost of a warm body, because it kept itself warmer than the water around it.
